headline.text: Printing money raises prices when the new money reaches people who spend it rather than hold it, in an economy that cannot simply produce more, and when it is expected to last.

k1-money-and-prices.text: Across countries and decades, faster money growth went with faster inflation: loosely in calm decades, steeply among fast printers.

sources.source: Lucas, R. E. (1996), 'Nobel Lecture: Monetary Neutrality', Journal of Political Economy 104(4)
sources.passage: Thirty-year averages for 110 countries (McCandless & Weber): the points lie roughly on the 45-degree line; the simple correlation between inflation and money growth is .95 (M2), .96 (M1), .92 (M0).

sources.source: Borio, C., Hofmann, B. & Zakrajsek, E. (2023), 'Does money growth help explain the recent inflation surge?', BIS Bulletin 67
sources.locator: p. 1, key takeaways; p. 3, Graph 2 and footnote 5
sources.passage: The link between money growth and inflation 'is one-to-one when inflation is high and virtually non-existent when it is low'; the same result holds with the thresholds set on excess money growth rather than inflation.

sources.source: Teles, P. & Uhlig, H. (2010, rev. 2013), 'Is Quantity Theory Still Alive?', NBER Working Paper 16393
sources.passage: For countries with low inflation, the raw relationship between average inflation and money growth 'is tenuous at best'; below 12 percent inflation the points 'no longer assemble nicely around a line'.

sources.source: Rolnick, A. J. & Weber, W. E. (1997), 'Money, Inflation, and Output under Fiat and Commodity Standards', Journal of Political Economy 105(6); FRB Minneapolis Quarterly Review 22(2) reprint
sources.passage: Under fiat standards (14 countries, 15 periods) the slope through the grand means of long averages is close to unity; the authors caution that the facts do not show causality.

k2-cases-us-targets.text: The Federal Reserve targeted the money stock from October 1979, de-emphasised M1 in October 1982, and downgraded M2 in July 1993.

sources.source: Federal Reserve, FOMC Record of Policy Actions, meeting of 6 October 1979
sources.passage: A shift in open market operations to 'supplying the volume of bank reserves estimated to be consistent with the desired rates of growth in monetary aggregates'.

sources.source: Federal Reserve, FOMC Record of Policy Actions, meeting of 5 October 1982
sources.passage: 'much less than usual weight be placed on movements in' M1 during the quarter.

sources.source: Greenspan, A., testimony before the Subcommittee on Economic Growth and Credit Formation, House Committee on Banking, 20 July 1993
sources.passage: 'At least for the time being, M2 has been downgraded as a reliable indicator'.

k2-loose-in-calm-times.text: In calm times the link is loose, because the demand for money moves: people hold more money when holding it costs little, and central banks supply what is demanded at their interest rate.

sources.source: Benati, L., Lucas, R. E., Nicolini, J. P. & Weber, W. (2016), 'International Evidence on Long Run Money Demand', NBER Working Paper 22475
sources.passage: Long-run money demand: for low-inflation countries the data often prefer velocity linear in the short rate (Selden-Latane); the demand for M1 moves with the cost of holding it.

sources.source: McLeay, M., Radia, A. & Thomas, R. (2014), 'Money creation in the modern economy', Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin 2014 Q1
sources.passage: The Bank of England 'does not directly control the quantity of either base or broad money'.

sources.source: Greenspan, A., testimony before the Subcommittee on Economic Growth and Credit Formation, House Committee on Banking, 20 July 1993
sources.passage: M2 'has been downgraded as a reliable indicator of financial conditions'; the relationships between money and income, and money and prices, 'have largely broken down'.

k3-other-printings.text: The Bank of Japan targeted banks' reserves with it from March 2001 to March 2006, until consumer prices excluding fresh food stopped falling, which it judged done in March 2006, and in April 2013 set out to double the monetary base, from {{boj_base_2012}} to an expected {{boj_base_2014}}; defending its floor against the euro, the Swiss National Bank took its assets to {{snb_assets_gdp}} of GDP; British inflation reached {{uk_cpi_2011_09}} in September 2011, put down by the Bank of England to VAT, energy and import prices, after it had bought {{boe_apf_held_2011}} of assets with new reserves; in October it raised the total to {{boe_apf_2011}}.

sources.source: Bank of Japan, 'New Procedures for Money Market Operations and Monetary Easing', 19 March 2001
sources.passage: The operating target changed to 'the outstanding balance of the current accounts at the Bank of Japan', in place 'until the consumer price index ... registers stably a zero percent or an increase year on year'.

sources.source: Bank of Japan, monetary policy decision of 9 March 2006
sources.passage: The operating target changed back 'to the uncollateralized overnight call rate'.

sources.source: Bank of Japan, 'Introduction of the Quantitative and Qualitative Monetary Easing', 4 April 2013
sources.passage: 'It will double the monetary base ... in two years'; the base 'was 138 trillion yen at end-2012' and 'is expected to reach ... 270 trillion yen at end-2014'.

sources.source: BIS Quarterly Review, March 2015, overview 'A wave of further easing'
sources.passage: The defence of the floor 'had caused the SNB's total assets to surge to 87% of GDP in December'; 'on 15 January ... the SNB discontinued the cap'.

sources.source: BIS Quarterly Review, September 2011, 'Global growth and sovereign debt concerns drive markets'
sources.passage: Quoting the SNB on 6 September 2011: 'With immediate effect, it will no longer tolerate a EUR/CHF exchange rate below the minimum rate of CHF 1.20.'

sources.source: Bank of England, Inflation Report, November 2011
sources.passage: 'CPI inflation rose to 5.2% in September ... the elevated rate of inflation reflects the temporary impact of increases in VAT, energy prices and import prices.'; p. 5: 'the MPC increased the size of its asset purchase programme by £75 billion, to a total of £275 billion'; p. 10: in September 'Eight members voted to keep the stock of asset purchases at £200 billion'; in October, a further £75 billion 'by the issuance of central bank reserves'.

sources.source: Bank of Japan, monetary policy decision of 9 March 2006 (read 2026-10-08)
sources.passage: 'Concerning prices, year-on-year changes in the consumer price index turned positive.'

k4-capacity-and-lag.text: The same money meets different prices when output can rise than when it cannot, and an expansion read as temporary is held, not spent; in moderate inflations, monetary policy's peak effect on prices has come more than a year later.

sources.source: Batini, N. & Nelson, E. (2002), 'The lag from monetary policy actions to inflation: Friedman revisited', Bank of England External MPC Unit Discussion Paper 6
sources.passage: It takes over a year before monetary policy actions have their peak effect on inflation (UK and US, 1953-2001), a rule of thumb for countries that have had moderate inflation; the authors take no stand on whether money has a special role.

sources.source: Krugman, P. (1998), 'It's Baaack: Japan's Slump and the Return of the Liquidity Trap', Brookings Papers on Economic Activity 1998(2)
sources.passage: 'only temporary monetary expansions are ineffectual'; a monetary expansion perceived to be permanent will raise prices or output.

k5-2021-23.text: In 2021-23, strong demand, fed by transfers the central banks' purchases helped finance, met supply and energy shocks; how much the money itself added, scholars weigh differently.

sources.source: Blanchard, O. & Bernanke, B. (2023), 'What Caused the US Pandemic-Era Inflation?', NBER Working Paper 31417
sources.passage: The inflation 'largely reflected strong aggregate demand, the product of easy fiscal and monetary policies, excess savings accumulated during the pandemic, and the reopening'; most of the surge came as shocks to prices given wages.

sources.source: Borio, C., Hofmann, B. & Zakrajsek, E. (2023), 'Does money growth help explain the recent inflation surge?', BIS Bulletin 67
sources.passage: Countries with stronger money growth saw markedly higher inflation (beta 0.29 on 30 economies); the findings 'say little about causality', and money may capture the income effect of the fiscal transfer.

sources.source: Barro, R. J. & Bianchi, F. (2023, rev. 2025), 'Fiscal Influences on Inflation in OECD Countries, 2020-2023', NBER Working Paper 31838
sources.passage: About 80% of effective government financing came from the effect of unexpected inflation on the real value of public debt.

k5-our-weighing.text: That the money added to the 2021-23 inflation, beyond the fiscal demand that carried it, is our judgement: our cross-section cannot separate the two.

k7-who-gains.text: On cash the gain is the state's (the inflation tax on base money); on deposits that paid nothing the loss went to those owing at fixed rates below inflation, the state among them, and to banks through their spread.

sources.source: Buiter, W. H. (2007), 'Seigniorage', NBER Working Paper 12919
sources.passage: 'The inflation tax is the reduction in the real value of the stock of base money caused by inflation.'

sources.source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, press release of 24 April 2020 (Regulation D)
sources.passage: The six-per-month limit on convenient transfers from savings deposits deleted, so savings could be classed with checkable deposits.

p2-1-bands.text: By band of money growth, the slope rose with the pace: {{lr_x_s1}} at or below {{lr_line}} a year, {{lr_x_s3}} between {{lr_x_edge20}} and {{lr_x_edge30}}, {{lr_x_s5}} above {{lr_x_edge50}} (an exploration).

scope.measure: average inflation against average money growth, ten-year windows (slopes)
scope.population: every money with the data at both ends of a window (IMF, World Bank, ECB, FRED), by coverage only

p2-1-steeper-with-pace.text: Over 1950-2020, each point of base money growth went with about {{lr_base_mu_below}} of a point of inflation in decades below {{lr_line}} a year, and about {{lr_base_mu_above}} in decades above it; counted on broad money, the public's cash and deposits, with the line on its own growth, about {{lr_broad_mu_below}} below the line and {{lr_broad_mu_above}} above it.

scope.measure: average inflation against average money growth, ten-year windows (slopes)
scope.population: every money with the data at both ends of a window (IMF, World Bank, ECB, FRED), by coverage only

p2-10-shutdowns.text: In April 2020 unemployment reached {{csc_unrate_2020_04}}, the job losses of the virus and the measures taken against it; the Fed's purchases, announced in March 2020, answered that shock.

sources.source: Federal Reserve, FOMC statement of 29 April 2020
sources.passage: 'The virus and the measures taken to protect public health are inducing sharp declines in economic activity and a surge in job losses.'

sources.source: Federal Reserve, FOMC statement of 15 March 2020
sources.passage: Citing the coronavirus outbreak's disruption, 'the Committee will increase its holdings of Treasury securities by at least $500 billion and its holdings of agency mortgage-backed securities by at least $200 billion'.

p2-10-two-economies.text: 2008-14 and 2021 met different economies: unemployment stood above {{csc_unrate_line}} from {{csc_unrate_above8_from}} to {{csc_unrate_above8_to}}, peaking at {{csc_unrate_2009_10}}, while in 2021 it fell from {{csc_unrate_2021_01}} to {{csc_unrate_2021_12}}.

p2-2-base-against-broad.text: In {{csb_moneys}} economies' decades with both money growths at or below {{lr_line}} a year, mostly since 1990, each point of central-bank money growth went with {{csb_base}} of a point of inflation, each point of the public's money with {{csb_broad}}.

scope.measure: inflation per point of money growth, broad slope less base slope (OLS, clustered by money and currency union)
scope.population: decade windows with base and broad money growth both at or below 12% a year

p2-3-before-1950.text: Before 1950, in {{lr_1870_economies}} rich economies, inflation went with the Macrohistory Database's narrow money about {{lr_1870_mu_below}} of a point per point below the line; the fast-money decades were the world wars'.

scope.measure: average inflation against narrow money growth (base money, notes or M1 by country), ten-year windows
scope.population: 18 rich economies of the Macrohistory Database

p2-4-earlier-printings.text: Earlier American printings: the Union's greenbacks from 1862, legal tender not convertible into gold; the Fed's purchases of Treasury securities in the Second World War, its balance sheet peaking at about {{fed_bs_ww2_gdp}} of GDP, gold its largest asset, against just over {{fed_bs_2014_gdp}} in 2014.

sources.source: Willard, Guinnane and Rosen (1995), 'Turning Points in the Civil War: Views from the Greenback Market', NBER WP 5381
sources.passage: 'In early 1862, the United States government began issuing Greenbacks, a legal tender currency that was not convertible into gold'; the chance of redemption depended on the war's expected cost.

sources.source: Judson and Weiss (2026), 'A Brief Illustrated History of the Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet', FEDS Notes, 13 February
sources.passage: The balance sheet 'expanded dramatically during the Great Depression and through World War II ... peaking at about 22 percent of GDP'; at the onset of the war 'Treasury purchases expanded as a means to support wartime investment', though 'gold certificates remained the dominant asset component'.

sources.source: Judson and Weiss (2026), 'A Brief Illustrated History of the Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet', FEDS Notes, 13 February
sources.passage: 'The balance sheet size peaked at just over 25 percent of GDP in 2014'.

p2-4-largest-modern.text: In the Fed's monthly series of central-bank money, which starts in {{csc_base_first_month}}, the stock had grown at most about {{csc_pre2008_max_growth_74m}} over any {{csc_w1_months}} months, or {{csc_pre2008_max_growth_22m}} over any {{csc_w2_months}}, before 2008; it grew {{csc_w1_base_growth}} over the first printing and {{csc_w2_base_growth}} over the second.

scope.measure: growth of the monetary base (FRED BOGMBASE, vintage 2026-09-30)

p2-4-money-held-2020.text: From February to May 2020 the public's money rose by about {{csc_m2_feb_may_2020_tn}} while its velocity fell from {{csc_m2v_2020q1}} to {{csc_m2v_2020q2}}; in 2021 it grew {{csc_m2_growth_2021}} with velocity flat and nominal spending up {{csc_ngdp_growth_2021}}.

scope.measure: M2, its velocity (FRED M2V) and nominal GDP

p2-4-purchases-and-deficits.text: The Fed's Treasury purchases equalled about {{csc_w1_purchases_share}} of the federal deficits of fiscal years 2009-14 and {{csc_w2_purchases_share}} of those of 2020-21.

scope.measure: the Fed's Treasury holdings added over the whole fiscal years' federal deficits

p2-4-two-printings.text: The United States added about {{csc_w1_base_tn}} of base money over {{csc_w1_months}} months from 2008 and {{csc_w2_base_tn}} over {{csc_w2_months}} months from 2020; about {{csc_w1_reserves_share}} and {{csc_w2_reserves_share}} of it ended as bank reserves.

scope.measure: change in base money and in reserves (H.4.1, monthly averages)
scope.period: August 2008 to October 2014; February 2020 to December 2021
scope.population: the United States, the Federal Reserve's balance sheet

p2-5-cross-section.text: Across {{cse_n}} economies that started calm, faster broad-money growth in 2020-21 went with more inflation in 2022-23: about {{cs_e_broad_huber}} of a point per point (robust slope).

scope.measure: inflation per point of broad money growth (Huber robust slope, energy-import share controlled)
scope.period: broad money December 2019 to December 2021; inflation December 2021 to December 2023
scope.population: economies whose 2015-19 inflation averaged below 10% a year

p2-6-reserves.text: Banks cannot lend reserves to households and firms; since October 2008 reserves in the United States earn interest, which makes them close to bills.

sources.source: McLeay, M., Radia, A. & Thomas, R. (2014), 'Money creation in the modern economy', Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin 2014 Q1
sources.passage: QE buys mainly from non-bank financial companies, creating deposits for them; reserves are lent only between banks; newly created reserves 'do not, by themselves, meaningfully change the incentives for the banks to create new broad money'.

sources.source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, press release of 6 October 2008
sources.passage: The Board 'will begin to pay interest on depository institutions' required and excess reserve balances', effective 9 October 2008.

p2-7-big-inflations.text: In the four big inflations Sargent read, prices stopped when the deficit financing stopped, while the note circulation kept growing.

sources.source: Sargent, T. J. (1982), 'The Ends of Four Big Inflations', in R. E. Hall (ed.), Inflation: Causes and Effects, University of Chicago Press
sources.passage: Persistently large deficits financed by creating money impart the momentum; in each case 'the note circulation continued to grow rapidly after the exchange rate and price level had been stabilized'.

sources.source: Leeper, E. M. & Leith, C. (2016), 'Understanding Inflation as a Joint Monetary-Fiscal Phenomenon', NBER Working Paper 21867
sources.passage: 'Economists generally agree that historical episodes of high and volatile inflation rates inevitably have fiscal roots.'

p2-8-what-inflation-took.text: From March 2020, inflation took about {{csf_hh_lower}} to {{csf_hh_upper}} from the average US household's cash and checking deposits.

scope.measure: the loss of purchasing power on cash and on deposits that paid nothing, the reclassified savings read against other deposits' own path

what-to-watch.text: What to watch is not the size of the central bank's balance sheet but the money the public holds against its spending, whether the purchases pay for transfers or only swap bonds for reserves, and whether the economy can produce more.
